results.title: Food Desert Economic Data ~ North Minneapolis, MN
results.description:
This map shows an area in Minneapolis, Minnesota and the three nearest markets with healthy food for sale.  The United States Department of Agriculture describes a “food desert” as an area with “limited access to supermarkets, supercenters, grocery stores, or other sources of healthy and affordable food”.  That aptly describes this area.  
The three North Minneapolis markets are dispersed in a line from the north to the southeast, then south. The Income Data map shows a large cluster of light green blocks indicating households with average incomes of $14,600 - $58,200. This is one of two data clusters indicating average household income below $58,200. The other is southwest. There are a few random blocks of darker green (Avg. $58,200 - $101,700) within the northeast cluster and located adjacent the 3 supermarkets. The data blocks in the surrounding areas are autocorrelated and show increased income levels radiating away from the light green cluster. 
The Unemployment Data map shows a clustered pattern similar to the Income Data map. Also, the Income Data and Unemployment Data maps show a correlation between areas where unemployment is highest and average household income is lowest.  There are a few anomalies scattered randomly across the area.  On the Income Data Map the block just southwest of the center pin has a higher average household income than the surrounding blocks, but the Unemployment Data map shows a higher rate of unemployment than other areas with the same average income.  The block directly north of the same pin has the highest unemployment rate in the area at 28%. 
There is clearly a problem for the people living in this area. Even when the average household income is $40,000, when looking more closely at the breakdown for individual households within the specific tracts, many have a income of less than $15,000. The United States Census Bureau “sets income thresholds based on the number of people in a family. If a family's total income is below that number then every member of the family is considered in poverty.” In 2017 the poverty level for a family of three was $16,895. There is a large population residing in the neighborhoods west of the 3 supermarkets.  Since so many are living in poverty they probably do not have access to a vehicle. And the Minnesota climate is extremely cold during the winter months. U.S. climate data says the average high temperature for Minneapolis, in December, is 27°F (and it often drops below 0°).  The Lyndale Farmers Market is the market furthest south. There is fresh produce May through November and it’s open daily from 6am-1pm. However they limit their hours in winter making wholesome foods even scarcer for the many needy people in the area.

results.title: A Consensus on the Urban Census
results.description:
Gentrification is a global phenomenon where members of an urban counterculture move to less desirable neighborhoods for a better deal at city living. In the United States, creatives arrive in the newly gentrifying neighborhoods and make the area desirable until it becomes a site of interest for corporations. Gentrification can positively impact neighborhoods through public art installations, cleaner streets, and lowered crime rates. But the slow process of housing costs rising and the displacement of low-income residents of color is an unfortunate truth. Can this process be stopped, or at least identified and contained? In this project, I will attempt to visualize and analyze gentrification in Minneapolis by mapping census data.

Since I first noticed the impacts of gentrification on my childhood neighborhood of Andersonville, Chicago, I have wanted to create an interface that shows how urban demographics have changed over time. Based on development trends, the interface would show where the next gentrification hotspots may be. Aside from my technical knowledge, what has held me back is how difficult it is to measure this process. This is a problem that the field of geography faces. While gentrification may cause racial and economic shifts, many of its impacts cannot be quantified. For example, an eroding sense of community and an unwelcome feeling experienced by longtime residents is a subjective and common occurrence.
results.snippet: Can gentrification in Minneapolis be identified by analyzing and visualizing census data?

results.title: Food Insecurity and Income
results.description:
According to the United States Department of Agriculture, food insecurity is defined as the limited and/or uncertain availability to nutritionally adequate and safe foods. Food insecurity is an issue as it can negatively impact the health and wellbeing of residents in urban and rural areas. Individuals with insufficient access to fresh and healthy foods are more likely to face physical health problems such as malnutrition, obesity, and cardiovascular disease. Individuals facing insecurity may also be forced into sourcing food in ways which are deemed socially unacceptable such as shoplifting or dumpster diving. To examine how and why food insecurity impacts populations, let us consider the city of Minneapolis as an example.

Census tracts in red represent areas where at least 18% of residents face food insecurity, tracts in white represent the national average, and tracts in blue represent areas where food insecurity is under 18%. As we can see there is a significant portion of the city of Minneapolis which faces above average food insecurity. More specifically, the Camden, Near North, Phillips, and Powderhorn neighborhoods are impacted the most. Food insecurity is not only an issue for urban centers, it is something which impacts the entire state of Minnesota.
results.snippet: An analysis on the correlation between food access and income in the city of Minneapolis.

results.title: Minnesota Voting Trends And How They've Shaped Our State
results.description:
Our story map analyzes different factors that influence how Minnesotans Vote. We thought of our topic when we were looking through topic ideas online. Both of us were interested in the political topics, and knew then that we wanted to do something relating to that. After we figured out our interest, we needed to decide on a specific topic. Finally, after lots of thinking, we decided to do a project on how Minnesota votes in Presidential elections, and why this is.


Most of our research was done online, with news reports, articles, and tables of data. We made a google document to take notes on, and immediately got to work. One problem we originally encountered, was what part of our broad topic we were going to be working on. At first, we took notes on all the different types of elections, but realized that we needed to narrow our focus. We decided to do the Presidential elections, because they have the most information and are very impactful to our country in whole. In our research, we rarely had issues with a lack of sources, and were able to get tons of notes on a variety of websites. We mostly researched before we began or story map, but also did some along the way when we needed more specific pieces of information.


After we finally finished taking our notes, we moved on to making maps. The first map that we created was about education levels in Minnesota, organized by county. We created a spreadsheet and started inputting information. One of the most challenging things about this map was the amount of counties that we had to find the location of. For each county we had to go into arcGIS and find the coordinates, which was very tedious because we had to repeat this 87 times. Once we downloaded this file as a csv, we put it into arcGIS, and it was finished. We did this again for our income map, which was much easier since it was the same format as the previous map, and we could use the same coordinates from our education map. The last map that we personally created was the county comparison map. For this map, all we had to do was add two map notes in two different counties. The rest of the maps we made used map layers that were created by Esri, so there were no problems there.


Once our maps were constructed and research was mostly done, we created our Story Map on Esri. The first map that we made didn’t work, and was difficult to get into our group to work on together. We eventually got the kinks worked out, and were able to get it fully functioning. Our map was the series style, and we used the kind with the scrolling tabs on the side. Once we became more familiar with the story map and figure out how we wanted to organize it, we decided we wanted to make a second story map to have one inside our story map. The second one had all of our voting factors, and it goes with the county comparison tab on our first map.
